questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to Italy as I like the Italian culture.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I can really recommend Venice. It was a huge experience, since the city is so different from any other city. It is really special that there are no cars or bikes and that you commute by boats. There are so many cultural activities to do in Venice and the ESN community (the volunteers doing activities for erasmus students) is really well organized.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
It was quite easy to find and get the needed information as Ca' Foscari is very good at sending emails with everything you need. If you need to look up courses, you can use this link:
https://www.unive.it/data/9639/
. The academic calendar is stated here:
https://www.unive.it/pag/36141/
.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I participated in the intro meeting held from the university and the campus tour. You can also choose to get a local buddy from the university that can help you answer your questions about the city or the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: To get a "rejsekort" (Unica carta) to the boats (vaporetto in venezian), you need to go some of the bigger "stations" for example Ferrovia (the train station) or Rialto. Here, you need to bring ID (I brought passport) and you need to have the signed certificate from Ca' Foscari stating that you are a student in Venice. I think it costs 10 euros to get the Unica carta and then 25 euros each month for unlimited transport in Venice and to the busses to Mestre.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It is really difficult to find housing in Venice due to the lack of accommodation. I will recommend sending an email to all the dorms on the island, to contact the housing office of Ca' Foscari and maybe also contact the rental agency SoloStudenti. I will really suggest people to try find housing on the island or at Lido, as I cannot (!) recommend anyone to stay in Mestre (it is not a safe place).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is really special to live on the island, as you become a part of the very few locals in Venice. However, Lido is also a great choice, as there are many boats sailing from Lido all day (also during night) and you have easy access to the beach.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I lived at the Buon Pastore dormitory near St. Pietro in Castello. It was such a good experience, even though you typically share a room in Italian dormitories. It was really cheap (350 euro per month) and it was easy to take the boat from either St. Pietro or Giardini. All the girls living at the dorm were extremely nice and the communication with the administration was very easy.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is easy to register, as Ca' Foscari just send you a step-by-step-guide that you have to follow.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You just need to follow carefully all the mails that you receive.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could always write to the international office of Ca' Foscari.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: You don't need to register for classes only for the exams. There are no limits to the amount of students in the classes so that is not a problem.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just check you KU mail.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really liked the courses at Ca' Foscari as they have many courses that combine sustainability and finance.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some of the lectures were a bit difficult, as the professors expect the student to participate, raise your hand, answer sudden questions etc. However, the exams were generally easy and the grading is very generous.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is expected to participate in the class discussion much more than at KU, however, if they know you are an exchange student, they may give you an easy time. In Italy, you cannot see the history of exams (they have no archive), so instead you get one mock exam to practice. Be aware, that you can typically do voluntary extra work (for example a presentation) and then add 1-3 points to you grade, but typically these extra points can ONLY be added if you already pass the exam in which they doesn't matter when you only have to pass the exam (however, you might get some friends from the course by doing the extra work...).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: I took Economics of risk and agent behaviour, Financial Reporting, Advanced instruments for sustainable finance and impact financing - 1 and 2, and Climate change and finance: Metrics to assess risks and opportunities.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I can recommend Economics of risk and agent behaviour. The teacher was really motivated, good at explaining the theory and spoke english well. The exam was also quite easy, and I would say that it is the closest course to a typical KU course. 

I cannot recommend Financial Reporting, since the professor was not very nice and it didn't feel like safe learning environment. 

Advanced instruments for sustainable finance and impact financing - 1 and 2 was interesting, however the professor didn't manage to present it in an interesting way, but she was really nice. 

Climate change and finance: Metrics to assess risks and opportunities was also interesting, but be aware that you have to weekly homework. On the other hand, the exam questions is drawn from 30 questions (incl. the answer) that the professor gives you beforehand.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I think the prices are quite fair in Venice, of course around Rialto bridge or Piazza San Marco it is tourist prices, but you can find good places at the Jewish Neighbourhood in Cannaregio, Fondamente de la Capuzine in Cannaregio, around Campo Santa Margeritha in Dorsoduro (where all the students go for spritz!) or at Via Garibaldi in Castello just to mention some bigger/more famous/easy accessible places.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Spritz (or select as the locals drink) is very cheap

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The ESN community in Venice has so many activities, just go follow them on Instagram and show up to their events. That is where you get all your international friends. Go to Morion (the only night club in Venice) on Friday evenings, go to the football games at St. Elena, buy the museum card (Venezia Unica City Pass), visit Teatro La Fenice to reduced price by showing you student card, go to the beach on Lido and just go explore the city.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I joined the running club. You can also find them on Instagram and join their Whatsapp group. It is free to run with them and I got a couple Italian friends there. They run from both Piazzale Roma on the island and from Mestre.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to all the ESN events and join the running club! In that way, you get both international and Italian friends.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I will recommend going to Padova (very close) or Bologna and Firenze. It is also easy to go to the Dolomites for hiking in the weekend.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The Italians are very open-minded and welcoming so I felt quickly at home in Venice.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Sign up for the buddy program, join the running club, or do the extra voluntary work in groups in the courses.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Some of the Italian girls at my dorm didn't speak english, but luckily I quickly learned a bit Italian and then we also just used Google Translate.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I liked the more laid-back approach that the Italians have to life.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Don't live in Mestre
2) Go to ESN events and mingle with the international students
3) Explore all the cultural stuff in the city

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Even though it is a bit confusing with the boats in the beginning, you will quickly get a hang of it, and then it will be one of the things you are going to miss most about Venice. And compared to other Italian transportation, the boats are actually almost always on time!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: My friends from all around the world

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I think it was the lack of information about the exams provided by the professors. As they are more laid-back, they think that everyone will be fine by showing up on the exam day and get the relevant information there, but I got quite nervous about not knowing exactly how it was going to be... However, in the big picture it didn't really matter, because I had such a good stay.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I can really recommend Venice, it is so special!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
